About the role

The Communications and Signal Processing Group at Imperial College has two part-time openings in machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) to design a new layer of communication infrastructure using high-altitude platform systems (HAPS) to provide communications services to ground users. The positions are funded by the ARIA EndAP programme: https://aria.org.uk/opportunity-spaces/adaptive-machines/enduring-atmospheric-platforms/funded-projects?tabId=ta3&cardId=ai-enabled-haps . The post-holders will join a diverse team with expertise in network AI and optimization, wireless communications and networks, aircraft design and deployment regulations to leverage the strengths of different HAPS platforms, determine the best fleet composition, and coordinate platform movements for energy efficiency, resilience, and adaptability to traffic demands of ground users.

To begin, we will study how multiple HAPS platforms should be strategically moved and positioned in three-dimensional airspace to provide the optimal service coverage and meet communication quality of service (QoS) requirements for ground users subject to navigating weather, energy, and regulatory constraints. A robust backhaul network will be designed to connect HAPS with each other, and with terrestrial and satellite networks, ensuring efficient network-wide connectivity and flexibility.
We aim to develop a reinforcement-learning framework for joint optimization of air-vehicle design, real-time control, and provisioning of communication services under changing weather, energy availability, and regulatory constraints. Our goal is to develop novel distributed RL algorithms for each HAPS will function as an autonomous, distributed RL agent, making independent but cooperative control decisions to optimize its position, resource allocation, and operational strategy in real time. 
This post will also participate in assessment of alternative power architectures and operational constraints to ensure consistent power availability for both individual HAPS units and entire fleets. We will develop robust fleet operational strategies to identify minimum viable fleet sizes and configurations under varying weather, deployment, and coverage requirements. Furthermore, to use the designed algorithm in practice, we will evaluate how physical constraints, such as payload size, weight, and power supply, and techno-economic tradeoffs affect the optimal HAPS system designs. We will adapt and validate the developed HAPS technologies across multiple fleet platforms.
The positions are an excellent opportunity for researcher with strong background in machine learning, wireless communications and communication networks. Strong analytic skills are expected.

What you would be doing

Research Duties include:

To plan and carry out research in accordance with the project aims and timeframes.
To propose and investigate new techniques, algorithms and architectures for network design, optimization and orchestration.
To verify and characterize system performance both analytically and in realistic simulated testbeds.
To collaborate and cooperate with other research staff both within and outside Imperial College working on related projects funded by the UK EPSRC.
To act as the representative for Imperial College in meetings, conference calls and conferences.
To present research at conferences, workshops, open days and meetings, and publish research results in journals.
To develop a sound understanding of ethical and health and safety regulations, and the responsibilities of themselves and their colleagues

What we are looking for

Education

Research Associate: Hold a PhD in Electrical Engineering, Computer Science, Mathematics, or a closely related discipline, or equivalent research, industrial or commercial experience
*Candidates who have not yet been officially awarded their PhD will be appointed as Research Assistant.

Research Assistant: PhD (or equivalent) candidates in Electrical Engineering, Computer Science, Mathematics, or a closely related discipline.

Experience

Machine learning (ML) and/or optimization for communication systems
Development, implementation and verification of ML algorithms in code
Algorithm development and performance analysis of data-driven decision-making systems

Knowledge

Machine learning and optimization techniques
Key technologies in wireless communication systems
Networked and distributed systems

What we can offer you

The opportunity to continue your career at a world-leading institution and be part of our mission to continue science for humanity.
Grow your career: gain access to Imperial’s sector-leading dedicated career support for researchers as well as opportunities for promotion and progression.
Sector-leading salary and remuneration package (including 39 days off a year and generous pension schemes).
Be part of a diverse, inclusive and collaborative work culture with various staff networks and resources to support your personal and professional wellbeing.

Further information

Please note that job descriptions cannot be exhaustive, and the post-holder may be required to undertake other duties, which are broadly in line with the above key responsibilities.

For any specific queries regarding the post please contact Prof Kin K. Leung (kin.leung@imperial.ac.uk)

Research Associate in Equitable Energy Systems

The role

This is an opportunity to work within the ambitious and impactful SHINE project, bringing together an international, transdisciplinary team to understand and improve the design of energy systems to have a positive impact on well-being and inclusion in The Gambia and Ghana. Working with academic institutions, internationally recognised organisations, and government ministries in Ghana, The Gambia, South Africa, Nepal and Brazil, the project will research and develop design methodologies and pilot energy interventions that seek to drive an inclusive energy transition.

What will you be doing?

The role holder will closely collaborate with the international partners to implement pilot energy systems in The Gambia and Ghana, which will include overseas fieldwork. The role holder will follow a mixed-method approach, collecting and examining predominantly qualitative data (including but not limited to interviews, focus groups, participatory mapping) from the pilot energy systems. In addition, they will be integral in designing and refining the holistic SHINE framework incorporating data from the pilot energy systems. They will work closely with the broader SHINE team to understand the implications of the data and develop methods to further understand the linkages between energy systems and well-being.

You should apply if

You will have a strong background in qualitative social science, ideally within the energy access sector, with the ability to conduct participatory methods as well as code, analyse and draw out key themes from interviews, focus groups, and transect walks that can be used to inform energy system design and future policy. You will also be able to analyse quantitative data, with the ability to use programmes like SPSS, MATLAB, REDCap and Microsoft Excel to draw out statistical measures. You should have experience working with international, transdisciplinary teams, so you must be able to communicate clearly, effectively, and respectfully across cultures, languages and disciplines. You will need to support the project administration, including developing ethical applications and ensuring that the project adheres to relevant University of Bristol requirements for research studies as well as necessary reporting. You will likely need to travel as part of this post, with visits to the partners in The Gambia and Ghana to collaborate on the pilot studies. Previous international travel experience is advantageous.

About us

Recently re-founded, the Department of Engineering is rapidly expanding into a world-class research and teaching department. Research currently focuses on robotics, telecommunications and biomedical engineering, but we are looking to establish new research themes.

We offer both undergraduate and postgraduate teaching, with a distinctive approach, combining both traditional teaching methods with modern, project-based learning, catering for the needs of our students and the industries in which they will work.

As a new department we have invested in new laboratories and maker space at the centre of the Strand campus in the heart of central London.

For more information:  https://www.kcl.ac.uk/engineering

The position is funded by an EPSRC research grant whose vision is to offer an attractive, flexible, low-carbon, scaled, sustainable Demand Responsive Transport by offering optimised, scaled routing and scheduling and integrating dynamic pricing with behavioural insights.

About the role

We are advertising for a Research Assistant or Research Associate position at King’s College London to work with Prof. Rym M’Hallah (King’s), Prof. Christine Currie (University of Southampton), Prof. Julia Bennell, and Dr. Chiara Calastri (University of Leeds) on large scale optimization techniques and revenue management with applications to Demand responsive transport systems.

The researcher will undertake research specifically developing routing and scheduling methodologies. Of particular interest is the development and investigation of exact and heuristic optimisation approaches for routing and scheduling using stochastic data. The researcher will be expected to engage in problem formulation, algorithm implementation (using appropriate solver software and programming languages), experimental design and analysis of results. In addition, the research includes embedding pricing methodologies (already developed) and behavioural insights (provided through another work package).

The successful candidate will be part of a research team with five other members. You will be expected to engage in regular online and in person meetings, develop presentations for academic and practitioner audiences, and write reports and journal articles.

The successful candidate should have a PhD (or have submitted a thesis and awaiting results) in Operations Research, Mathematics, Computer Science, Industrial Engineering, or Transport Engineering and be proficient in a mainstream programming language. Candidates with a Masters degree in relevant subject areas will be considered for a Research Assistant role.

The post will be based within the Department of Engineering, located at the Strand campus of King's, in the centre of London. The post involves routine working on campus at King’s and regular in-person meetings at Leeds and Southampton.

This is a full-time post - 100% full time equivalent. It will be offered on a fixed-term contract until 31st May 2027.

For an informal discussion about the role, please contact Professor, Rym M’Hallah.

About you

To be successful in this role, we are looking for candidates to have the following skills and experience:

Essential criteria

1.       For grade six Research Associate role - PhD qualified in relevant subject area (or pending results): Operations Research, Mathematics, Computer Science, Industrial Engineering, Transport Engineering. For grade five Research Assistant role - Masters degree in relevant subject area 

2.       Strong foundation in mathematics and deep knowledge of exact optimization techniques, heuristics and matheuristics   

3.       Experience of using and implementing mathematical programming (including constraint programming)  

4.       Proven track record of high-quality research publications in peer reviewed journals and international conferences  

5.       Excellent programming skills (including Python and off-the-shelf solvers)  

6.       Experience in using and implementing stochastic optimization and simulation  

7.       Excellent written and oral communication skills  

8.       Ability to work co-operatively within a team striving for collective excellence. 

Desirable criteria

1.       Good understanding of the concepts of revenue management 

2.       Understanding of Behavioural Science   

Knowledge of digital twin systems

Liverpool John Moores University (LJMU) is a distinctive, unique institution, rooted in the Liverpool City Region and with a global presence. Our students and staff, past, present, and future, are the beating heart of our city and can be found in every corner of every industry and community. We couldn’t exist anywhere else and have shaped the city in which we belong. Working with the people of Liverpool to improve lives and support communities is at the heart of why we were founded and why we exist today.

We are now looking for highly motivated Research Fellow (PDRA) to develop and conduct individual and/or collaborative research projects. This is a 24-month fixed-term appointment supported by the EPSRC-funded Maritime and Last Mile Net Zero (MaLaMi) Place Based Impact Acceleration Account, under the supervision of Professor Zaili Yang, offering an opportunity to contribute to innovative research and practical solutions for maritime and last-mile decarbonisation.

You will support the development and application of quantitative and data-driven approaches to address challenges in maritime transportation, sustainable logistics and decarbonisation, with particular focus on Engineering Net Zero, Artificial Intelligence (AI), digitalisation and data. The work will contribute to evidence-based decision-making, the development of practical solutions and the advancement of sustainable transport systems.

Key responsibilities include: 1) contributing to scoping, feasibility assessment and proof-of-concept development for maritime and last-mile decarbonisation projects; 2) supporting the development and application of quantitative and data-driven models, including modelling, simulation, optimisation and machine learning; and 3) assisting in the development, testing and evaluation of analytical tools, prototypes and demonstrators, working collaboratively with academic researchers and external partners.

You should possess a good honours degree and a PhD (or equivalent professional experience) in transport, logistics, engineering, operations research, data science or a relevant discipline. You must demonstrate strong quantitative research and data-analysis capabilities, proficiency in programming or analytical tools, and the ability to disseminate research findings through high-quality publications in international journals and refereed conferences. Experience with research or innovation projects related to maritime decarbonisation, sustainable logistics, AI, digitalisation or proof-of-concept development is preferred.

You will work as part of the EPSRC-funded MaLaMi programme, collaborating with an interdisciplinary team of researchers, investigators and external partners, within the Liverpool Logistics Offshore and Marine Research Institute (LOOM) at Liverpool John Moores University, UK. LOOM enjoys an international research reputation in maritime risk studies, https://www.ljmu.ac.uk/research/centres-and-institutes/loom.

In return, we offer an excellent benefits package including generous annual leave entitlement, pension scheme, induction, and development support as well as family-friendly policies.

This is an exciting time to join the university as we deliver the LJMU Strategy 2030 and its vision of LJMU as an inclusive civic university transforming lives and futures, by placing students at the heart of everything we do.

If you feel that this is the role you have been looking for and your skills and experience can make a real difference at LJMU, we look forward to hearing from you.

The School/department is committed to promoting equality and diversity, including the Athena SWAN Gender Equality charter for promoting the career of women in STEM (science, technology, engineering, mathematics) in higher education. We particularly welcome applications from women for this post and all appointments will be made on merit.

Fixed-term: The funds for this post are available for 3 years in the first instance.

The Janeway Institute at the Faculty of Economics, Cambridge University has a Postdoctoral Research Fellowship available for candidates working on areas of economics related to transmission mechanisms and economic policy. Eligible candidates include those who have recently been awarded a doctoral degree or expect to receive their degree by September 2027.

The Fellowship is for a maximum period of three years, but candidates can request a shorter term of one to two academic year(s) if this is a better fit for their career plans. The Fellowships will be based at the Janeway Institute. The Janeway Institute was created to develop new fundamental ideas, methods and research which push the frontier of economics. Fellows also have the possibility of joining a Cambridge College.

We welcome applications from researchers working on areas of economics related to transmission mechanisms and economic policy. This includes but is not limited to research into the contributions of firms and sectors in the aggregate economy; inquiries into how heterogeneity across households and firms shapes economic outcomes and contributes to economic growth; studies of the conduct and impact of monetary and fiscal policy in closed and open economies; and investigations of other economic factors that shape the economy and contribute to economic growth.

For more information see https://www.janeway.econ.cam.ac.uk/

Successful candidates should demonstrate an ability to develop their own research ideas and indicate how they can contribute to the transmission mechanisms research group in Cambridge. It is expected that successful candidates' work will be at the cutting edge of the research frontier with a view to future publications in world leading journals.

Successful candidates who have not yet received their PhD by September 2027 will be appointed on University Grade 5 as Research Assistants, starting at Grade 5, spine point 38 (£34,610 per annum). Upon award of the PhD, their salary will be upgraded to Grade 7 as Research Associates (Fellowships), starting at Grade 7, spine point 41 (£37,694 per annum) in the first year. In the second year, the salary will rise to spine point 42 (£38,784), and in the third year to spine point 43 (£39,906).

Janeway Teaching Fellowships, which provide supplemental remuneration on top of the Research Fellowship salary listed above, are available for those interested in gaining valuable teaching experience and contributing to the learning environment. These opportunities are contingent on the Faculty's needs and the candidate being suitably qualified. Further details, including the amount of additional remuneration, can be discussed during the interview process.

Applications should consist of:

A curriculum vitae; expression of interest cover letter outlining how you would be able to contribute to the Janeway Institute in light of your research interests; a job market paper; supplementary material such as other available research papers.

Three references will be sought upon receipt of application.

Click the 'Apply' button below to register an account with our recruitment system (if you have not already) and apply online.

Queries may be directed to Marion Reusch, Janeway Institute Administrator, ji@econ.cam.ac.uk

Please quote reference JH50885 on your application and in any correspondence about this vacancy.

The University has a responsibility to ensure that all employees are eligible to live and work in the UK.

About the role

King’s College London is a world leading research-intensive university with a strong international profile and a long-standing commitment to addressing major societal and global challenges.

This role is based within the Faculty of Life Sciences & Medicine, in the School of Immunology & Microbial Science in the Department of Infectious Diseases. It brings together expertise across microbiology, immunology, clinical sciences, data science and artificial intelligence.

The Department offers a highly interdisciplinary and collaborative environment, with strong links to clinical partners and access to outstanding research infrastructure and cross faculty initiatives.

About us

This is an exciting project Supported by the BBSRC. Antibiotic resistance (ABR) is one of the biggest public health challenges of our time. In 2019, 1.27 million deaths were attributed to antibiotic resistant bacteria. The gut microbiome is composed of harmless symbionts, commensal bacteria, and opportunistic pathogens, all of which play crucial roles in human and animal health and disease. In physiological conditions the gut microbiome is stable, but when perturbative events occur (e.g., dietary changes, infections, stress, antibiotic administration) the population of microbiota changes, influencing health and protection against further colonisation. These changes may involve new resistant bacteria becoming permanent residents or transferring resistance to the commensals). The core concepts underlying our project are: to gaining a better understanding of how the gut microbiome changes as consequence of infection, co-infection, or treatment (including the development of resistant traits) is a fundamental starting point towards understanding the mechanisms of inception and spread of endemic diseases and antimicrobial resistance.

The research associate will be responsible for developing, implementing and applying artificial intelligence, machine learning, deep learning and data-mining methods to address complex research questions. They will lead the analysis of large-scale, heterogeneous datasets, including sequencing, sensor, biological and medical data, and ensure robust, reproducible computational workflows.

The postholder will be responsible for developing and applying AI methods across the following areas, demonstrated through scientific publications or other academic/industrial achievements:

Generative AI (text and numerical data; excluding image, audio, video generation)
Agentic AI, orchestration, and adaptive systems (continuous feedback, dynamic reasoning, self-optimisation)
AI methods for mining, classifying, and forecasting from heterogeneous data sources
Spatial-temporal statistics/modelling from heterogeneous data (Bayesian hierarchical models, autoregressive models, random fields)
Sequence/time-series modelling and language models, particularly transformer architectures
Explainable AI methods
Causal AI methods
Machine learning

This is a full-time post 35 Hours a week, and you will be offered a fixed term contract until 31st August 2028.

This entitlement, from the Concordat to Support the Career Development of Researchers, applies to Postdocs, Research Assistants, Research and Teaching Technicians, Teaching Fellows and AEP equivalent up to and including grade 7. Visit the Centre for Research Staff Development for more information.

Job id: 161305. Salary: £45,031 - £48,607 per annum, including London Weighting Allowance.

Posted: 21 October 2026. Closing date: 18 November 2026.

Business unit: Natural, Mathematical & Engineering Sci. Department: Engineering.

Contact details: Dr Oya Celiktutan. oya.celiktutan@kcl.ac.uk

Location: Strand Campus. Category: Research.

Back to job search

About us

We are recruiting a motivated Postdoctoral Research Associate to join CO-STAR (CO-designing Socially inTelligent Assistive Robots for Future Healthcare), a research programme bringing together King’s College London, Guy’s and St Thomas’ NHS Foundation Trust, and the Royal Academy of Engineering. CO-STAR aims to advance socially intelligent assistive robots for future healthcare, combining cutting-edge research in artificial intelligence and robotics with human-centred co-design and real-world clinical deployment. We are looking for a candidate who can join the project in January 2027 or soon thereafter.

The successful candidate will join the Department of Engineering at King’s College London and become a member of the Social AI & Robotics Lab (SAIR), led by Dr Oya Celiktutan. They will work closely with researchers, engineers, healthcare professionals, patients and other stakeholders at Guy’s and St Thomas’ NHS Foundation Trust (GSTT), providing a unique opportunity to conduct cutting-edge robotics research in close partnership with a major NHS organisation.

SAIR conducts research in multimodal machine learning and human-centred embodied AI, with a particular focus on developing autonomous agents that can perceive, understand and interact effectively with humans. The lab’s research addresses challenges in multimodal perception, human behaviour understanding and forecasting, robot learning, navigation and manipulation, and socially aware human–robot interaction.

SAIR’s research has been supported by the Royal Academy of Engineering, EPSRC, the Royal Society, and EU Horizon programmes, as well as through industrial collaborations. The lab’s research has received several distinctions, including the Best Paper Award at IEEE RO-MAN 2022, the NVIDIA CCS Best Student Paper Award Runner-Up at IEEE FG 2021, and First Place and Honourable Mention Awards at the ICCV UDIVA Challenge 2021. 

About the role

Imagine a future where robots meaningfully assist people with limited mobility and support patients and clinicians across healthcare environments. Assistive robotics has the potential to transform independence, wellbeing, and the delivery of care. Advances in AI are rapidly expanding what robots can perceive, understand, and do, bringing this future closer than ever. Yet a critical gap remains between technical capability and real-world deployment: robots still struggle to understand human behaviour, adapt to complex social situations, and operate safely and appropriately alongside people. Using the hospital as a living lab to advance human–robot interaction and integration with clinical workflows, the CO-STAR project aims to bridge this gap.

CO-STAR will engineer the next generation of socially intelligent assistive robots that can interact naturally with people while meeting the demands of real-world healthcare environments. 

The successful candidate will play a key role in shaping and delivering the research programme, working across human–robot interaction, machine learning, socially intelligent AI, and healthcare robotics. They will contribute to the design, development, and evaluation of robotic and AI systems and work closely with the multidisciplinary CO-STAR team and Guy’s and St Thomas’ NHS Foundation Trust to translate research advances into real-world healthcare settings. Please refer to the Job Description for further details about the role and the required application documents.

The successful candidate will be expected to:

shape and conduct high-quality multidisciplinary research in collaboration with the CO-STAR project team;
develop novel research in human–robot interaction, machine learning, and socially intelligent robotics;
contribute to the design, development, implementation, and evaluation of robotic and AI systems within the scope of the project;
disseminate research findings through high-quality publications and presentations at leading international conferences and journals;
contribute to activities that maximise the academic, clinical, and societal impact of the research.

This is a full-time, fixed-term post for 21 months, with the potential for extension up to a total of 42 months, subject to funding arrangements. The desired start date is January 2027 or as soon as possible thereafter.

Application Documents

Please read and follow the application instructions carefully. Applications that do not comply with the requirements below, including the specified page limits, will not be considered. Please submit only the requested documents, as additional or unsolicited materials may also result in rejection.

1. Curriculum Vitae (maximum 2 pages): Provide an up-to-date academic CV detailing your qualifications, research experience, technical expertise, and relevant achievements. Include a complete list of publications at the end of your CV (excluded from the 2-page limit) and highlight up to three publications that best demonstrate your research contributions.

2. Supporting Statement (maximum 3 pages): In the context of the CO-STAR project, provide a structured statement demonstrating how you meet the essential and desirable criteria outlined in the Person Specification.

•       Address each criterion individually, using its corresponding title (e.g., Essential Criterion 1, Essential Criterion 2).

•       Essential Criteria: Address all six essential criteria individually, providing specific evidence and examples.

•       Desirable Criteria: Address all four desirable criteria individually, providing relevant evidence or explaining your motivation where applicable.

•       PhD Completion Status: If your PhD has not yet been awarded, clearly state your current stage of study, expected thesis submission date, anticipated viva date (if known), and expected date of completion.

Your responses should be concise, evidence-based, and relevant to the CO-STAR project. Avoid general statements without supporting examples.

3. Academic Referees: Provide the names and contact details of two academic referees, preferably including your current or most recent research supervisor. Please indicate whether they may be contacted informally before the interview.

About you

To be successful in this role, we are looking for candidates with the following skills and experience:

Essential criteria

PhD awarded (or near completion*) in Engineering, Computer Science, Robotics, Artificial Intelligence, or a closely related discipline.
Strong research background in socially aware or human-centred AI, machine learning, robotics, and/or human–robot interaction.
Strong publication record in high-quality peer-reviewed journals and/or international conferences, such as ICRA, IROS, RA-L, CoRL, AAAI, NeurIPS, CVPR, HRI, or related venues, commensurate with career stage.
Excellent programming skills, particularly in Python, and hands-on experience with deep learning frameworks and models.
Practical experience with the Robot Operating System (ROS), physical robotic platforms, and/or robot simulation environments.
Excellent written and verbal communication skills, with the ability to communicate complex technical concepts effectively to both academic and non-academic audiences.

Desirable criteria

Experience of collaborative research, particularly in multidisciplinary environments involving researchers, engineers, and other project stakeholders.
Experience with multimodal machine learning, foundation models, and/or neuro-symbolic AI approaches.
Experience conducting human–robot interaction studies or evaluating robotic systems with human participants.
Experience of, or strong motivation for, collaborating with healthcare professionals, patients, and other stakeholders in real-world clinical environments.

Downloading a copy of our Job Description 

Full details of the role and the skills, knowledge and experience required can be found in the Job Description document, provided at the bottom of the page. This document will provide information of what criteria will be assessed at each stage of the recruitment process.

* Please note that this is a PhD level role but candidates who are close to completing their PhD will be considered. In these circumstances the appointment will be made at Grade 5, spine point 30 with the title of Research Assistant. Upon confirmation of the award of the PhD, the job title will become Research Associate and the salary will increase to Grade 6. 

Further Information

At King’s, we believe that the diversity of our community and a culture that is welcoming, open, inclusive and collaborative, are great strengths of the university.

The Equality Act of 2010 protects the rights of our students and staff and provides a framework to fulfil our duties to eliminate unlawful discrimination, harassment and victimisation and in addition, to advance equality of opportunity and foster good relations between those who share a protected characteristic and those who do not. At times, this will include balancing rights and beliefs that can feel in tension.

We are committed to free speech and to academic freedom, believing that our foundational purpose as a university, is to create spaces where a wide range of ideas, including ideas that are controversial, can be discussed and debated, and where members of our community can express lawful views without fear of intimidation, harassment or discrimination.

When engaging in the robust exchange of ideas, we ask that our community is mindful of our Dignity at King’s guidance.

We ask all candidates to submit a copy of their CV, and a supporting statement, detailing how they meet the essential criteria listed in the person specification section of the job description. If we receive a strong field of candidates, we may use the desirable criteria to choose our final shortlist, so please include your evidence against these where possible.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is evolving rapidly, and we recognise its growing role in professional work. Applicants may use AI tools to support preparation of their application, for example to research the role or structure written responses. However, applications must reflect the applicant’s own work and experience. We reserve the right to close adverts early due to the volume of applications we receive. While the closing date may change, all adverts will close at 23:59 to allow sufficient time for applications to be submitted on that day.

We encourage you to apply at the earliest opportunity to avoid disappointment as once we have closed a vacancy you will be unable to submit your application.

To find out how our managers will review your application, please take a look at our ‘How we Recruit’ pages.

Position Title: Research Assistant - Marie Curie, Mechanical and Electrical Design of Industrial Heat Pump Compressors – 16996 

Department/College: Department of Engineering/College of Engineering, Design and Physical Sciences 

Location: Brunel University London, Uxbridge Campus 

Salary: £50,508 per annum inclusive of London Allowance - without any pension contributions 

Hours: Full-time 

Contract Type: Fixed-term for 36 months                                   

Brunel University London was established in 1966 and is a leading multidisciplinary research-intensive technology university. For more information please visit: https://www.brunel.ac.uk/about/our-history/home 

The Department of Engineering delivers programmes in Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, Chemical Engineering, Electronic and Electrical Engineering, and Civil and Environmental Engineering. It has a wide portfolio of undergraduate and postgraduate taught and research programmes and is active in delivering transnational education. The department has a thriving research culture with substantial research facilities supporting the delivery of world leading impactful research. 

We are seeking to appoint a research assistant who will undertake research towards a PhD degree in Mechanical Engineering. The project objectives are to develop models for the design and analysis of turbo-compressors suitable for industrial high temperature heat pumps (IHTHPs). The focus will be on compressor system mechanical and electrical design considering sealing and cooling of components. The models will be validated using Finite Element and Thermal Analysis tools. 

Candidates must hold at least a first degree or a Master-degree in Mechanical Engineering or a relevant subject. 

This project is part of a Marie Sklodowska Curie Actions (MSCA) ITN aiming to train 15 PhD candidates within the newly funded project: Industrial Decarbonisation Using Innovative Low-Grade Heat Upgrade (HeatMinds). The overall aim of the work programme is to undertake cutting-edge multidisciplinary research and development to make a step change in the understanding of Industrial High Temperature Heat Pump technology. The successful candidate will start on 1 April 2027. 

Candidates must not have worked or studied in the UK in the last three years.

The Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence (CFI) at the Institute for Technology and Humanity are inviting applications for a Postdoctoral Research Associate. This is an exciting opportunity to work within a research project in trustworthy AI, led by Professor Adrian Weller. This is a fixed-term post where funding is available for two years.

The research project investigates how to develop fundamental theory and methods that enable machine learning systems to be deployed in a trustworthy manner. The project spans human-AI interaction, fairness, transparency, privacy and other approaches to optimising deployed AI systems as human-machine teams. The postdoc will conduct research developing and evaluating methods at the frontier of trustworthy AI, validating them on real-world problems in partnership with domain experts and stakeholders, and publishing and presenting results at leading venues in machine learning (such as NeurIPS, ICML and ICLR), AI ethics and society (such as FAccT and AIES), as well as policy fora.

Applicants should have completed, or be near completion of, a PhD in Computer Science, Information Engineering, Statistics, Machine Learning or a closely related field, with expertise in one or more areas of trustworthy AI, such as human-AI interaction, fairness, transparency and interpretability, privacy, or robustness. A strong understanding of machine learning methods, together with excellent mathematical and programming skills, is required.

CFI is a highly interdisciplinary research centre addressing the challenges and opportunities posed by artificial intelligence (AI). Based at the University of Cambridge, the Centre has close links with industry, policymakers, and many academic disciplines.

The role holder will also be able to have a desk in the Machine Learning Group in Engineering.

In order for your application to be considered, please upload the following:

Curriculum Vitae (CV)
Covering Letter explaining your interest in and aptitude for the position
Sample of professional writing
Names and contact details of two referees who are familiar with your work

If you upload any additional documents which have not been requested, we will not be able to consider these as part of your application.

Informal enquiries about the role are welcomed and should be directed to Professor Adrian Weller at aw665@cam.ac.uk.

For questions on the application process, please contact the School's HR Team on sahhr@admin.cam.ac.uk.

The closing date for applications is midnight (GMT) on Sunday 08 November 2026. Interviews are planned for the second half of November, subject to change.

postings.advert_text:
We invite applications for a Postdoctoral Research Associate in Mathematical and Statistical Methods for Genome Privacy in the Department of Applied Mathematics and Theoretical Physics at the University of Cambridge. The successful candidate will join the research group of Dr Gamze Gursoy and work on developing new mathematical and computational methods for privacy-preserving human pangenome references.

Human pangenome references provide increasingly rich representations of human genetic diversity, but their scale and structure also raise important questions about how information contributed by individuals can be protected. This project will develop new approaches at the intersection of graph algorithms, statistical methodology, optimization, privacy, and computational genomics, with the broader goal of enabling useful population-scale genomic references while limiting disclosure of sensitive information about the individuals represented within them.

Depending on the successful candidate's interests and background, research directions may include differentially private construction and analysis of pangenome graphs, privacy-aware graph algorithms and representations, statistical characterization of privacy-utility trade-offs, optimization of algorithms for large genomic graphs, and development and benchmarking of methods on human pangenome data. There will be considerable freedom for the successful candidate to help shape the scientific direction of the project.

We are particularly interested in candidates with a strong background in one or more of the following areas:
- statistics;
- graph theory or graph algorithms;
- mathematical or numerical optimization;
- differential privacy or related areas of data privacy;
- algorithms and theoretical computer science;
- computational genomics, bioinformatics, or pangenomics.

We do not expect candidates to be experts in all of these areas. Applicants with deep expertise in one area and a strong interest in learning and working across the others are strongly encouraged to apply. In particular, we welcome applications from statistics, mathematics, optimization, privacy, or algorithms who are excited about applying their methods to fundamental problems in human genomics, as well as researchers from computational genomics who are interested in developing expertise in privacy.

The project is highly interdisciplinary. The successful candidate will have opportunities to collaborate with Professor Po-Ling Loh in the Statistical Laboratory, Department of Pure Mathematics and Mathematical Statistics (DPMMS), particularly on statistical, optimization, and differential privacy aspects of the work. There will also be opportunities for interaction and collaboration with researchers in the broader Human Pangenome Project community.

The postholder will be expected to develop and manage their own research with guidance from the PI, contribute actively to the intellectual life of the research group, and communicate their work through publications, presentations, seminars, and conferences. They will join a collaborative group working broadly across computational genomics, statistical genetics, privacy-preserving computation, and trustworthy methods for genomic and biomedical data.

Applicants should have completed, or be close to completing, a PhD in statistics, mathematics, computer science, computational biology, bioinformatics, genomics, or a related field. Evidence of strong quantitative, computational, or methodological research is more important than prior experience in any particular application area. Strong programming skills and an interest in interdisciplinary research are desirable.

The funding requires that candidates must not have been UK residents during the 24 months before the start date, nor be currently employed by a UK organisation or its overseas campuses.

The appointment is for two years in the first instance.

Click the 'Apply' button below to register an account with our recruitment system (if you have not already) and apply online.

Please indicate the contact details (including their email addresses) of two academic referees on the online application form and upload a full curriculum vitae and a description of your recent research (not to exceed two pages). Please ensure that at least one of your referees is contactable at any time during the selection process and is made aware that they will be contacted by the Mathematics HR Office Administrator to request that they upload a reference for you to our Web Recruitment System; and please encourage them to do so promptly.

For informal enquiries, please contact Dr Gamze Gursoy at gg584@cam.ac.uk.

If you have any queries regarding the application process, please contact: LE51229@maths.cam.ac.uk.

Heilbronn Research Fellowships in Pure Mathematics, Data Science, and Quantum Computing
The role

The Heilbronn Institute for Mathematical Research invites applications for Heilbronn Research Fellowships. Fellows divide their time equally between their own research and the classified research programme of the Heilbronn Institute. Research areas of interest include, but are not restricted to, Algebra, Algebraic Geometry, Combinatorics, Data Science, Number Theory, Probability, and Quantum Computing. Fellows have previously been appointed with backgrounds in most areas of Pure Mathematics and Statistics, and Mathematical/Theoretical Physics.

We expect to make up to 10 appointments at the University of Bristol, Imperial College London, King’s College London, UCL, and the University of Manchester. These appointments will mainly be in Pure Mathematics with up to two of the appointments at the University of Bristol in Data Science or Quantum Computing.

The salary range is £46,874 - £52,517 (or local equivalent) depending on previous experience, plus the London weighting where appropriate. There is a salary supplement of £3.5K pa, in recognition of the distinctive nature of these Fellowships. Payment of this supplement is conditional on a PhD thesis having been accepted in final form.

The positions are 3 years with fixed-term funding until 2030 with a preferred start date of 1 October 2027. Extensions of up to three years may be available, which can be held at a wider range of universities in the UK.

What will you be doing?

Fellows divide their time equally between their own research and the classified research programme of the Heilbronn Institute, thus enjoying opportunities to engage in collaborative work as well as individual projects.

Fellows join a cohort of around 50 Heilbronn Research Fellows that includes some of the leading early-career mathematicians in the UK. Expert mentoring will be provided by the host department, with a national programme of career development events overseen by our Associate Chairs, who are based in the School of Mathematics at the University of Bristol, Imperial College, and the University of Manchester.

The internal research programme is determined by the Head of HIMR in conjunction with GCHQ. Fellows are presented with a range of challenging mathematical problems and are given the facilities and support to contribute to one or more of them, frequently as part of a collaborative team.

You should apply if

Due to the nature of the Institute's work, Fellows must apply for a national security clearance at an appropriate level before appointment. Applications are open only to UK residents who are UK, or dual UK nationals: applicants are welcome to contact the Heilbronn Manager at himr-recruitment@bristol.ac.uk to discuss eligibility before applying.

The Heilbronn Institute is a supporter of the LMS Good Practice Scheme aimed at advancing women’s careers in mathematics and we particularly welcome applications from women.

Additional information

Applications will be made through mathjobs.org

Applicants will need to submit a cover letter, indicating the institutions where they prefer to hold their Fellowship from the above list of partner universities. In addition, we require a CV and a one-page statement of external research objectives over the 3 year Fellowship term. Applicants must arrange for three letters of reference to be uploaded to the mathjobs.org website, prior to the closing date.

The application deadline is 11.59pm GMT, Sunday 8th November 2026.

We anticipate holding interviews over the 11th - 14th of January 2027. 

For informal queries please contact: himr-recruitment@bristol.ac.uk 

Our strategy and mission

 

We recently launched our strategy to 2030 tying together our mission, vision and values.

JOB DESCRIPTION

 

Job Title:  Research Assistant (Cloud-Based AI)

College/Professional Service:  College of Creative Arts, Technology and Engineering

	

Grade:  E

Location:  High Wycombe Campus / Hybrid

	

Hours:  84 hrs in total from Nov 26 to Jul 27

Responsible to:  Project Lead

Responsible for:  No line management needed

Job Purpose:

To support delivery of the funded research project ‘Cloud-Based Smart Digital Twin for Predictive Calibration Management of Weighing Instruments’, by designing, developing and implementing a cloud-based digital twin system that combines mechanical engineering knowledge, AWS cloud architecture and AI/ML techniques to predict and manage the calibration of weighing and measurement instruments.

 

 

Main Duties & Responsibilities of the role:

Design and implement a complete cloud-based system on Amazon Web Services (AWS) to support the digital twin project, covering architecture, development, deployment and maintenance.
Apply mechanical engineering principles, including sensor behaviour, material degradation and calibration processes, to inform the design of the digital twin model for weighing and measurement instruments.
Develop and apply Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) techniques to build predictive capabilities, such as fault prediction, condition-based maintenance and optimisation.
Write and maintain robust, well-documented code, primarily in Python, to support system development and data analysis.
Collect and record the data required from weighing scales (e.g. sensor readings, load and calibration data) to support model development, testing and validation of the digital twin.
Investigate and, where appropriate, implement AWS IoT TwinMaker or similar digital twin platforms to realise the smart digital twin functionality.
Use MATLAB or similar simulation and modelling tools to validate system performance and calibration predictions, where required.
Contribute to the testing, validation and continuous improvement of the predictive calibration management system.
Prepare technical documentation, reports and presentations summarising project progress, methodology and results for the research team and funders.
Collaborate effectively with academic supervisors, project partners and other researchers to ensure timely delivery of project milestones.
Comply with relevant legislative and other requirements (e.g., the Data Protection Act 2018 and GDPR; Health and Safety; UKVI; and Equality and Diversity) in all working practices.
Such other duties temporarily or on a continuing basis, as may reasonably be required.

Senior Research Associate in Vegetation and Fire Modelling
 Apply
The role

The Postdoctoral Research Associate will work on the Copernicus Fire and Land-Atmosphere Modelling of Emissions (CoFLAME) project. CoFLAME will deliver scientific and technical advances to better account for interactions between wildfires and vegetation, improving estimates of wildfire emissions and natural CO₂ fluxes, while enhancing the forecasting of fire activity, fire probability, and fire spread.

At the University of Bristol, you will develop new theoretical and modelling frameworks to quantify vegetation recovery, mortality, and ecosystem legacy effects following fire. This work will combine data synthesis, model development, and analysis to deliver new process-orientated insights into post-fire ecosystem dynamics and the role of vegetation legacies in shaping land-atmosphere carbon exchange and ecosystem resilience under future climate change.

You will join the research lab of Professor Martin De Kauwe at the University of Bristol and will collaborate closely with an international team of researchers within the Copernicus Fire and Land-Atmosphere Modelling of Emissions (CoFLAME) project. Coordinated by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF), the consortium brings together leading scientists from the Finnish Meteorological Institute (FMI), GEOVILLE, NILU (Norway), the Royal Netherlands Meteorological Institute (KNMI), and the Portuguese Institute for Sea and Atmosphere (IPMA).

Hybrid working is available and can be discussed at interview.  This is a full-time (100%) position but appointment at 80% time would be considered.

What will you be doing?

You will contribute to the Copernicus Fire and Land-Atmosphere Modelling of Emissions (CoFLAME) project by developing and applying new approaches to represent how vegetation responds to and recovers from wildfire. Working at the interface of ecosystem science, Earth system modelling, and remote sensing, you will investigate the impacts of fire on vegetation structure, carbon cycling, and ecosystem recovery. The role will involve developing and testing new model representations of post-fire vegetation dynamics, analysing observational and satellite datasets, and collaborating with international partners to improve the representation of fire-vegetation interactions in next-generation land surface models and forecasting systems.

You should apply if

You have:

A PhD (or soon to be awarded) in mathematics, vegetation modelling, physics, atmospheric science, or similar quantitative discipline.
Significant experience in ecosystem, vegetation, land surface, or Earth system modelling, ideally with applications to wildfire, disturbance, or ecosystem recovery.
Demonstrated programming/computing skills in a Unix/Linux environment.
Strong research and publication track record (relative to career opportunity)
Excellent verbal and written communication skills.
Demonstrated ability to work effectively as part of a team and independently in a research environment.

postings.advert_text:
A position exists for a Research Assistant in the Department of Engineering, to work on mechanics of fusion materials. The post holder will be located in Central Cambridge, Cambridgeshire, UK.

We are starting a new research project focused on developing damage-tolerant materials for space and fusion-energy applications with an emphasis on refractory, body-centered cubic alloys, and high stacking fault energy alloys. Materials used in space and fusion systems must retain their structural integrity under extreme combinations of mechanical loading, temperature, and irradiation. These materials are often very brittle, but new processing techniques, including but not limited to additive manufacturing, can potentially mitigate this issue. The project will investigate the fundamental mechanisms that govern deformation and damage in these materials and use this understanding to identify new approaches to their design. The role holder will conduct experimental research to characterise how candidate materials deform plastically (if at all) and resist fracture.

The work will involve performing mechanical characterisation including tensile, toughness and fatigue testing at room and elevated temperatures, performing electron microscopy characterisation including electron backscatter diffraction and transmission electron microscopy, and analysing/interpreting the resulting data. The candidate will be familiar with ASTM E399, E1820, and E647, dislocation mechanics, and microscopy techniques. The job will also include developing equipment including a micronotcher, vacuum-furnace and cryogenic testing system. The findings will be used to establish a first principles understanding and for the development of materials with improved resistance to damage and neutron irradiation.

The role holder will work closely with other members of the research group at Cambridge and with external collaborators, including at Lawrence Livermore National Labs. They will be expected to contribute to group meetings, present their findings, prepare research publications, and assist with grant administration.

The skills, qualifications and experience required to perform the roles are wide. The specific skills include excellent laboratory skills and data analysis capabilities.

The applicant is expected to have at least a Bachelor's degree in Engineering Science or Materials Science and Engineering. A Master's degree is preferable.

Membrane-based separations are central to addressing major sustainability challenges, from securing critical metal supplies for the energy transition to enabling energy-efficient water treatment. Developing the next generation of membrane processes requires predictive computational models that connect molecular-scale phenomena to system-level performance. However, the thermodynamics and transport behaviour of concentrated, multi-ion aqueous solutions remain poorly understood, limiting rational membrane design and process optimisation.

The Department of Chemical Engineering and Biotechnology (CEB) at the University of Cambridge welcomes applications for a Postdoctoral Research Associate to work on a UKRI Future Leaders Fellowship project developing computational models for selective ion transport in complex aqueous mixtures. The research combines molecular simulation, thermodynamic modelling, and continuum transport theory to build predictive frameworks for membrane-based ion separations.

The role will involve molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and density functional theory (DFT) calculations to understand ion-solvent and ion-membrane interactions, alongside the development of continuum-scale transport models. This is an opportunity to be a member of a new research group working at the interface of molecular simulation, chemical thermodynamics, and membrane science.

You will report to Dr Akshay Deshmukh (PI), a UKRI Future Leaders Fellow at CEB. You will work alongside an experimental PDRA and collaborate with international project partners. You will have access to CEB's world-leading facilities and the broader Cambridge research ecosystem, including the Cambridge Centre for Data-Driven Discovery.

The Institute of Astronomy (IoA) and the co-located, interdepartmental Kavli Institute for Cosmology, Cambridge (KICC) at Cambridge University are internationally renowned for a uniquely stimulating and multi-disciplinary research environment. One topic where Cambridge has a long history is black holes, the most extreme environments in nature, and laboratories where strong gravity, plasma physics and high-energy astro(particle)/physical processes meet. The research group of Prof. Sera Markoff (Plumian Professor) studies these systems across the full black hole mass scale, combining GPU-accelerated supercomputer simulations and semi-analytic modelling with data from world-leading facilities including the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT). Her group sits at the nexus of several international efforts: a growing Cambridge node, where this post is based (currently expanding over the coming years into a fully-fledged team of students and postdocs); an established group at the University of Amsterdam of several postdocs and students; her ongoing ERC Synergy Grant project 'Blackholistic', with partner groups at Oxford, Radboud University in Nijmegen, the University of Turku, the University of Namibia and the University of South Africa; and major international collaborations including the EHT and the Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory (CTAO). Via the ERC project, the group is also involved in commissioning a new 14-metre radio telescope in Namibia, the Africa Millimetre Telescope.

The group's research is built on a developing portfolio of in-house software: a GPU-accelerated general-relativistic magnetohydrodynamics (GRMHD) simulation code (in C, with GPU acceleration primarily on NVIDIA and AMD hardware); a GR ray-tracing code (in Julia) that produces images and spectra from those simulations, and is designed to conduct Bayesian parameter inference; semi-analytic jet and accretion modelling codes (in C++, with a Python interface) that are being integrated into the open-source Gammapy framework for use across the CTAO community and beyond; and increasingly building on other imaging and analysis frameworks used within the EHT Collaboration. These codes run on local, national and international high-performance computing (HPC) facilities.

This part-time 0.5 FTE Research Software Engineer (RSE) role will provide the professional software engineering capability at the centre of this network and will suit someone excited to work at the interface between modern software engineering and some of the most cutting-edge research in astrophysics.

The role-holder will establish and manage version-controlled repositories for all group software, deploy and optimise the codes on available HPC facilities, and embed good software practice across a distributed, international team through documentation, testing, code review and training. The role has a strong outward-facing dimension: coordinating shared code development with partner institutions and contributing the group's codes to community open-source frameworks used by international collaborations.

The purpose of the role is to ensure that the group's research software is reliable, performant, well-documented and reproducible; that development remains coordinated with partner groups as shared codes evolve; and that software engineering expertise is retained within the group as projects and personnel change. The role also offers clear scope for growth: the role-holder will be encouraged to engage directly in the group's research, helping develop new computational methods and contributing to publications, with responsibilities that can expand as the Cambridge node grows.

Click the 'Apply' button below to register an account with our recruitment system (if you have not already) and apply online.

In particular, the role-holder's responsibilities will include:

Establishing and managing reliable version-control infrastructure for the group's codes, including migration of legacy repositories. Defining repository structure, branching, access and release workflows so that all group software is secure, documented, citable and reproducible.

Liaising with partner development groups at other institutions to track external development branches of shared codes. Planning and carrying out the integration of selected external developments into the group's versions, coordinating builds and testing.

Setting up, testing and optimising the group's numerical simulation codes on local, national and international (US/CAN/EU) HPC clusters using AMD and/or NVIDIA GPUs (e.g., via CUDA, HIP, OpenCL, or similar). Carrying out application profiling and benchmarking, and contributing technical cases and support to group proposals for acquiring more HPC computing time.

Designing, coding, verifying, testing and documenting new physics capabilities within the group's codes, together with the research team, profiling and optimising their performance.

Investigating, prototyping and implementing machine-learning and advanced statistical methods (e.g. improved sampling for Bayesian parameter inference, surrogate models/emulators, simulation-based inference) to accelerate the group's modelling and inference workflows; evaluating their performance and implements improvements.

Supporting development of the group's semi-analytic modelling codes (C++ with a Python interface) through performance optimisation and branch management, and planning and carrying out their integration into the open-source Gammapy framework, adhering to community coding standards, so that they can be adopted across the CTAO community and beyond.

Implementing automated testing, continuous integration and documentation across the group's codebases. Providing advice, guidance and training to researchers and students in both Cambridge and Amsterdam to promote adoption of software engineering best practice.

Actively maintaining specialist knowledge and providing detailed advice to group leader Prof. Markoff on software strategy, computing resource planning and data-management plans for grant proposals and reports.

Within the group's research goals, building on and refining ideas for developing and evaluating new computational methods, collaborating with researchers on their application to open problems; reporting on work carried out and potentially contributing material of publication quality to group publications.

Click the 'Apply' button below to register an account with our recruitment system (if you have not already) and apply online.

Please indicate the contact details of three professional referees on the online application form and upload a full curriculum vitae (CV), list of publications (if you have such) and a research/technical experience statement (this research/technical experience statement being three pages max in 11pt font).

The closing date for applications is: 23:59 BST on Monday 9th November 2026.

Referees will be requested to provide references by the same date. Where permission is given by the applicant, references will be requested prior to the vacancy closing. Applicants are asked to inform their referees that they will receive a reference request communication including a link to upload a reference to the University of Cambridge recruitment system by the application closing date.

Applications will be reviewed after the closing date and interviews are provisionally planned for: w/c 30th November 2026.

We anticipate that this 0.5 FTE post is equivalent to circa 18.5 hours per week, flexibility in exact working hours per week may be required. As a guide, the General Board expects the average full-time working week for academic-related employees to be in the region of 37 to 40 hours, therefore a part-time, 0.5 working week can be considered on average to be 18.5 to 20 hours per week.

For any queries regarding the application please contact: hr@ast.cam.ac.uk. Informal enquiries may be addressed to Professor Sera Markoff via her EA, Joanna Carruthers, at plumianprofea@ast.cam.ac.uk.

Please quote reference LG50949 on your application and in any correspondence about this vacancy.

The University of Cambridge is a signatory to the San-Francisco Declaration on Research Assessment (DORA), and in recruitment or promotion evaluations will assess research on the basis of its merits rather than the journal or venue in which it is published.
